That right wing sub-controversy made it a treat to read an article in this newspaper earlier this week, headlined 'Here’s What Greeks Think of Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey.’ (It’s Their Story, After All.)'

Reporter Niki Kitsantonis described the reactions of the actual Greeks who have seen and commented on the film, which has provoked mixed reactions and a variety of critical assessments in Greece as elsewhere.

The the overall response appears to have been largely positive. A few angry far right Greek nationalists have attacked the film on the usual grounds of wokeness, and some viewers and reviewers have sniffed it was too "Hollywood," but on the whole audiences have responded with appreciation.

The Odyssey has long inspired artists to take their own shot at reworking the epic. From James Joyce (Greek scholars emphatically praised his Ulysses) to the Coen Brothers (Greek audiences loved O Brother, Where Art Thou?), it has been worked and reworked again and again. It never gets old.

He was brought up to be totally responsible for his own life by the men and women in the family who raised him - nothing is beneath him - cooking, cleaning, taking care of household and family things.  I am so fortunate. 
The other day we had a power outage and I went to call the electric company and he said "what's the rush, why are you getting all excited - I'm sure the neighbors will call" (we live in an HOA/connected townhomes community). It turned out that we were the only ones affected, due to our own tenant circuit breaker going bad - if we had waited, nothing would have been done by our neighbors. 
When we went to inspect the breaker outside, I said, "the power company told me we need to reset it ourselves - and why don't we open that black tab near our electric meter, since there doesn't seems to be any other visible circuit breakers in the utility closet?"  No, he tells me, that can't be it. So we called the company to send a technician out.  It turns out the circuit breaker was under that tab. 
That day, I wondered what brought on his responses to me.  I'm guessing it was that I "took his agency" as a man to respond first to a small emergency....but to me, I was just doing my part.  Lesson learned; it seems there is an inborn programming of that in men....and I don't mind recognizing and trying to work with that...it seems to be their nature:)

As an American of just over 81 whose life has exactly spanned our descent from being the Arsenal of Democracy which, with out allies, defeated the greater evil in human history to the social, political, religious, and financial morass in which now find ourselves - in which a man who would have felt quite at home in the Nazi hierarchy now inhabits the Oval Office for the second time, I find it hard to become interested in our defense budget. The only sure thing about building up our arsenal at any time after August 6th, 1945 is the increasing certainty that it will actually have to be used, possibly ensuring the end of human life on earth or at least resulting an even greater level of world-wide destruction than WWII. 

I lived through the years of MAD (Mutually Assured Destruction) including those 13 terrible days in October of 1962 when we waited, terrified, for resolution or Armageddon. If that didn’t scare us out of our endless saber rattling, it is hard to imagine anything that can. 

 The Swedish botanist, Carl Linnaeus named us Homo sapiens. It is hard to imagine a greater misnomer.

comments.name: Ithaca Reader

Here is my weird analysis about defense and defense spending. 

The Ukrainians have proven that it’s possible to hold the Russians at bay for around $100 billion a year. If they had an extra $100 billion they could also better protect their cities from Russian missile attacks. So the baseline for the larger European region to protect itself from Russian attack is spending a few hundred billion annually for European defense. 

So why are we in the US now asking for $1.5 trillion annually, when all it takes to defend against Russia, or by extension China, might only be a few hundred billion a year plus the cost of a nuclear retaliation option?

Of course, it’s because we also have to budget in the US for the illegal and unnecessary wars we like to launch every few years, but a line item for illegal wars at $100 billion annually might cover that.

I have seen few comments about the gift-giver not feeling as if the young recipient expressed sufficient gratitude.  

The Ancient Greeks had a number of words for love which can help us dampen our our desire for "something" in exchange when we give from ourselves in time, money or attention.  If you want your love to be AGAPE, do not expect something back.  Give because you want to help.  If you want PHILIA, do as the Ethicist suggested and value the young relatives as the people they are.  Don't seek the STORGE requirements of thank you letters, mentioning your generosity to others, etc.  Separate yourself from most of the people who write to the Ethicist and don't expect your family to act the way they are "supposed to". We don't use different parent names to distinguish because we're both their mom and even though we said our kids may want to down the line, they never have.  We're open to talking about that with people who ask, and I would encourage the questioner to do the same.  I'd also encourage the author not to make this assumption that this would not be possible.

I remember a kid in school asking me "Do both your parents really sleep in the same bed?" It was so important for me to see how my moms dealt with this, as it helped me deal with judgement and nasty comments of all kinds. So if you do quip back, remember you're teaching your kid how to respond. We always responded "That's none of your business" and ended the conversation. Also I called both my parents "Mom" my entire childhood. This sometimes led to confusion, but if that's what you want your kid to call you, you can make it happen and don't let anyone tell you otherwise.

 - The goal of the invasion was not a land grab but regime change. Russia only started to annex land in September 2022 - half a year into the war. The reason was probably that that made it easier to administer the conquered areas. 
 - Keeping Georgia out of the war is a sound strategy from the Georgian point of view. It has nothing to do with how democratic its leaders are.
 - Armenia did not revert to the West after it lost Nagorno Karabach. It did it much earlier. And the sorry fact was that the West did nothing to help it when it was attacked. In the meantime Russia's options were restricted. Armenia had recently refused to do military exercises with Russia and in the diplomatic game around Nagorno Karabach before the war it had followed Western advice and ignored Russia.

So anyone saying that people just need to  get used to the heat is ignoring reality.  I have been in the Montpellier region for over 30 years. We are used to heat here; temps have to be quite high before heatwaves are declared. I can tell you that the heat here since the end of May is awful. I don't have AC and my apartment is an oven. It used to be that without AC one would have a few uncomfortable weeks at the most. That is no longer the case. Traveling here now and trying to do anything besides sitting in the shade or in the water is not a good idea. Yes, more AC is needed. Yes, consider visiting off-season. I am acrophobic. My first memory of it was around 4 years old, walking across a mile long rope/plank bridge over a bottomless chasm atop Lookout Mountain. I remember clinging to my stepfather's leg as if my life depended on it, despite that I hated his guts.

But y'all really don't get it. Everyone has rational fears, including heights. They help us survive. But phobias are, by definition, IRRATIONAL "fears". You can't explain one away to a phobe. Phobes can't exercise it away.

The way I've learned to explain it to non-phobes is that it just plain makes my rear-end pucker. Think someone can explain that away? Think I can just learn to "relax?"

I began to realize I had a particular problem when I was an apprentice carpenter in my late teens. And particularly when the union kept sending me to a new bridge project. You guessed it, a mile high (not really) and (for real) several miles long. I made it through apprenticeship, but realized I wasn't getting used to it as I thought I would. It actually got worse, so I found a different calling.

I went back to Lookout Mountain a few years later though, determined to cross that bridge again. Piece of cake -- it was 10 feet long and 4 feet high.

“Like everyone on the tour of Ausable Chasm, a gorge carved into the Adirondacks in upstate New York, I wore a harness to catch me if I fell. Maybe it would save my life, but it didn’t do much to ease my anxiety.”

The operators of Adventure Trail and the manufacturers of the gear they use are counting on that gear saving you with 100% surety. The engineering involved in a via ferrata is also designed and maintained to that end. 

The real test for ability to handle heights is to move easily in an exposed position without any of the engineering or safety equipment. As a rock climber of 50+ years I marvel at the photos of old school iron workers casually moving around hundreds of feet in the air, working, eating lunch, whatever.

I recommend the author take the next step and actually go rock climbing with a good guide. Using the actual natural features of a climbing introduces a different and more meaningful challenge from a via ferrata that may distract you from your fear.

The climbing area known as the Shawangunks, near New Paltz, has a famous route called High Exposure. Its last pitch puts the climber 300 feet above the forest over plenty of air, albeit on easy climbing. As a teenager I free soloed it from bottom to top, never having climbed it before. I am confident I wouldn’t do that now, but on a rope I am confident it would not be too big a deal.

comments.body: That so many people were affected by the cyclospora outbreak purportedly tied to a single [albeit huge] farm, exposes the issues inherent with concentrating large portions of our food supply into a few producers or farms, where a single misalignment can affect thousands. Foods from these farms are transported in large quantities over long distances and they reach many more markets than ever before, and they're also processed into many end products such as single-serve or institutional-sized packaged salad mixes that have overtaken the produce sections all across our country and are often mixed with other lettuces, which can make them harder to trace than if they were sold whole to wholesalers and supermarkets. So even one problem in the chain along the way in the growing, handling, packaging, refrigeration, and distribution can easily cascade into widespread illness and even deaths and result in massive recalls and loss of wages and livelihoods for many. But the most widespread damage is the loss of confidence in our food suppliers and in the regulatory committees whose job it is to monitor and maintain the health and integrity of our food supply. Our country’s health leaders cannot be urging Americans to be healthy and to eat more fresh fruits and vegetables if it cannot adequately monitor all the actors in our increasingly vast and complex food supply network.

No idea where this outbreak is coming from but it's way too easy to blame Mexico, they are not alone. Taylor Farms and other big growers also have major produce farms in the U.S. 

It's worth watching the 2023 Netflix documentary, "Poisoned: The Dirty Truth About Your Food". Large livestock operations near produce farms likely continue to be a major source of outbreaks. Much of the documentary focus is on poultry farms and high salmonella risks but they also mention a couple of major known growing areas like Salinas Valley, CA and Yuma, AZ (where Taylor farms also operates). These areas create major contamination risks and I'm sure there are many more. Animal waste contains harmful pathogens like E. coli and many others. Irrigation systems, runoff and wind and dust soil movement carry the pathogens from nearby livestock operations that settle directly onto plants before harvest. These long known risks need to addressed. I'm not against big produce farms but they should not be anywhere near big livestock farming operations and all food should be easily traceable so when contamination is identified it can be quickly contained.

In summer and fall, I buy and support local growers. Winter I tend to eat less produce and select more frozen produce from lower risk growers without a recall history.

comments.name: Sarah
comments.body:
I am a biologist who teaches cell biology at a medical school. The term “peptide” just means a short chain of amino acids connected to each other with peptide bonds.

Some peptides are antimicrobial (kill bacteria). Some peptides are structural building blocks. Some peptides break down clots. Some enhance pain sensation. Many peptides are signaling molecules; meaning, cells use them to communicate with each other and to initiate chemical reactions and physiological changes.

The peptides these people want to sell and inject are hormones (signaling molecules that affect cells far away in the body). Most peptide hormones have more than one function and affect more than one type of cell. Some peptide hormones can stimulate normal cells and cancer cells in the same way, and some have different effects on healthy cells and pathological cells.

We do not know all the cells and tissues that are affected by these 7 peptides, or all of their functions (what reactions or chain reactions they trigger). As the article notes, the data are muddled by a lack of consistency in formulations. Meaning, vendors use the same name for different chemical variations, doses, and delivery methods.

Perhaps if we called these peptides “experimental hormones”, or better yet, “experimental hormones whose functions are not well understood”, maybe more people would understand why scientists and physicians want more research done before they are approved as medicine.

There is a native capacity for humans to develop which is often unappreciated.    Surrogate factors are used to define this or that segment by the way of skin pigmentation or skull form at times and the nature of Nazi collections of skulls for the analysis was popular to show the 'Aryan' superiority.

Stephen Jay Gould wrote the Mismeasure of Man which is also worth reading for its correction of what was one of the dead ends of prejudicial thinking of the past.

We need to see capacity as something hardly limited to this individual or that.    Humans can all excel if given the right circumstances so long as they suffer no genetic or developmental fault (not a racial one here but a true chromosomal or gene fault!) and no toxic exposure.

Even animals are more capable than we consider.   Researchers in my days of undergraduate education took it for granted that only humans had language.

We now speak of languages of whales, of great apes, of Parrots and Corvids (crows and ravens), of Elephants and of Prarie Dogs.

What we presume we know is what we have convinced ourselves that we understand.   Collective stupidity is often the nature of some holding of prejudice seeking a result it may determine by the nature of what it seeks to define as a criteria for capability.

Intelligence, when all is said and done, needs open-minded assessment of how it is measured and understood as even defined.

I worked for a decade as a DOE scientist at the Pacific Northwest Laboratories (now the Pacific Northwest National Laboratories).  While my work did not explicitly involve nuclear reactors or waste handling, one cannot work there without learning a great deal, and I also will say that one will not take a job there if one is strongly opposed to nuclear power, per se.

I want to say two things from my experience:

* nuclear power and its waste issues are very, very complicated, and unforgiving of errors.   You can be certain of one thing; anyone claiming it is simple or presenting "simple" arguments, either doesn't know, or is intending to gull you.

* all the really hard problems are chemistry and properties of materials, not the physics of reactor design.  

How many of you remember way back, before 9/11 ... when the LaRouche people would earbang travelers in airports about nuclear power?  They were a cult, and their mantra was "thorium molten salt reactors."   It's weird that nuclear reactor technologies have cults and fads.  Even weirder how long some of these endure.

The latest fad and huge flow of speculative investments is into SMR" "small modular reactors."   I have my doubts, too complicated to explain here.  But if SMRs can do anything, perhaps they can revive nuclear power for the largest freighters.   Call me when that has a decade of positive experience. 

And IMO, none of this should go forward until the USA settles long term waste disposal.

Further, the construction of nuclear power plants seems to be existentially linked to massive cost overruns.

Bill Gates, a smart guy who has done much for the world, is the most upbeat and vociferous proponent, but he is also a techno-nerd susceptible to the lure of gimmicky, upbeat technology.
I wonder how he would feel about having one of these time-bombs installed in his own neighborhood.

Japan came within a hair's breadth of having to evacuate the world's largest city, saved only by several fortuitous circumstances. Such consequences are not worth the cost, especially when alternative systems are available.

Some argue that Chernobyl and Fukushima were accidents unlikely to recur. But as the cliché has it, accidents happen.  There are also terrorists. And don't forget,  there is nuclear waste, with no means of disposal.

To encourage Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium while fighting a war to prevent its neighbor from doing so is simply another Trump irony, and another reason to nix it.

After reading dozens of depressing news stories in today's Times, I was cheered to see a piece about my adoptive home-town, Bangkok.

Bangkok is a wonderful place to live or to visit. The ferry along the Chaopraya will provide a very full day of entertainment with stops at ICON SIAM, Wat Phra Kaew, Wat Pho, Wat Arun, The Royal Palace, and Chinatown. Tour of the Jim Thomson House is excellent. Chatuchak Park weekend market is great if you like heat and crowds, but Tues - Thurs is the plant market which is a must visit for plant lovers. The shopping malls here can be a lot of fun. I like the three interconnected malls EM Quartier, EMSphere and the Emporium. And wonderful public parks like Benjasiri, Benjaketti, and Lumphini, not to mention my local park Santipap... just be careful not to step on the water monitors that wander freely.

Personally, I cannot imagine a visit to Bangkok without seeing the Nana Entertainment Complex with three floors of clubs, each offering a specialty... spanking, bondage, ladyboys, etc. An important part of the Bangkok experience.

I would not particularly recommend Phuket (it's okay). Much better to visit the group of islands Koh Samui (White Lotus), Koh Phangan, and Koh Tao (amazing diving and snorkeling).

I was totally floored by John Wogan's suggestion (companion article) of a low priced option in Chiang Rai costing $320/night. Very strange notion of low cost. You can stay in wonderful hotels in Thailand for cheap.

Ukraine's army is stronger with Federov overseeing things in any capacity; so he shouldn't get caught up in the semantics of rank, title or whether he's technically Defense Minister.
History will vindicate his efforts.

The case of US army general Patton during WW2 is a useful analogy; temperamentally egotistical, he was resentful of being subordinated to his former junior officer, Omar Bradley.
But as the ingenious operational whiz of the 3rd army, Patton achieved more glory destroying the German army than Eisenhower, Marshall or other paper-pushers who outranked him.

Federov appears most efficacious as a catalyst "force multiplier"; whose presence in processes/policies yields better results than if his innovation is sidelined.
Institutional changes can be slow and unwieldy, though; so having lodged his complaints, it's time for Federov to move on productively and accept the things he cannot change yet (with the wisdom to know the difference).

comments.name: Peter
comments.body: There comes a point where it is madness to throw good money after bad and allowing the premises to burn down twice indicates that we have reached that point with this building. The Glasgow School of Art is a living, vibrant institution and money should now be spent to create a home for it that meets the needs of a 21st century art college. Spending vast amounts of money to recreate something that would inevitably be a pastiche of the original does not serve well the needs of today's students. Scotland does not lack fine, historic buildings. What it does lack are modern public buildings of real architectural merit. Should the Glasgow School of Art not set an example by commissioning a contemporary Scottish architect to design a landmark building for this age.

comments.name: Kemlo Yaris
comments.body: I was fortunate to visit the School of Art as a tourist shortly before the first devastating fire. I am not an obvious person to be blown away by art or architecture but my hour or so in this building affected me in a way that no other building ever has done. I came away with an understanding of what great architecture means, not just bricks and mortar but the creation and expression of a coherent vision down to the last detail including everything from furniture to light fittings to door handles. If even I could come away in an hour thinking "I get it now!" then the value of this building to future young architects is incalculable and transcends politics. This is Scotland's Notre Dame and needs to be rebuilt.

comments.name: South Florida
comments.body: I was incredibly fortunate to have been able to work in Scotland at Hawthornden Castle, a retreat for writers and other artists outside Edinburgh, and I went to Mackintosh's  Glasgow School of Art before the first fire in 2014. I think it's almost impossible for anybody who has ever been in it not to be aware of its beauty and power and the quiet Beauty of its uniquely detailed interior. I have a picture in my home in the States of the Library, and I told a recent visitor who studied the image that it felt like a holy place. It occurs to me that if everybody who read about the situation prevailing for the school right now gave a single dollar, from every country in which this sort of article appears, in their currency, that would be millions of single dollars and they would add up and it might be possible to repair the building. This is the kind of thing that sounds child- like, but I wonder if the Scottish government would handle such an event, advertising and collecting the funds that would pour in if various newspapers in 50 countries asked their citizens to contribute that very small amount in their own currency.  I hope this strikes a chord in others who would happily donation very small funds. It would take a lot of donations, but there are lots of art lovers in the world. Let's go, y'all!

Catastrophic Wildfires and Apocalyptic Anxiety

Robert D. Stolorow

     Living in the Bay Area near San Francisco, I am far from the catastrophic wildfires that have been assaulting Los Angeles and the neighboring communities. Despite this long distance, I have been feeling an uncanny sense of danger, an anxiety that often appears in my body in the form of physical pain. The anxiety bears a similarity to my descriptions of reactions to the horrors of climate change, what I called “Apocalyptic anxiety” (Stolorow, 2024). 

     Such anxiety announces not only the loss of individual lives but also the destruction of human civilization itself, the nullifying of all future human possibilities. It thereby signals the ending of the historical process through which we make sense of our individual existences. Apocalyptic anxiety is thus often accompanied by a gripping sense of meaninglessness, a profound nihilism. “What’s the point?” is a refrain I can imagine haunting the rubble of the LA wildfires.

     I have previously discussed the use of metaphysical illusion to evade the catastrophic  consequences of climate change—specifically, the view of the earth as an indestructible and timeless metaphysical entity. A common way of evading the Apocalyptic anxiety evoked by the catastrophic wildfires is blame.  Blaming, especially as practiced by certain politicians, replaces powerlessness and vulnerability with aggression and illusory prosecutory power.

History is littered with autocratic systems that mistook early compliance for permanent submission.

By threatening to restrict model access, China hasn't sealed its supremacy; it has exposed its hand.

But it rests on a fundamental miscalculation: assuming that aggressive leverage won't provoke an equal and opposite reaction.

In the Mahabharata, the ancient Indian epic, there is a recurring truth: power and intellect unguided by humility act as a ticking time bomb—the grander the ego, the harder the fall. 

China’s calculated attempt to trap the world’s developer ecosystem on its models, only to suddenly pull back the curtain and restrict access, exemplifies this short-sighted hubris.

By threatening to sequester its latest models, Beijing is not securing permanent supremacy; it is simply ringing the alarm bell for the rest of the world.

The outside world must seize this opening, not with reactionary bans, but by building and funding an open, reliable, and secure A.I. foundation that global builders can actually trust.

It is a fact that the majority of its incumbent political establishment (Liberal Democratic Party - LDP) are direct descendants of samurai-turned-politicians from that time. Abe's maternal grandfather, Nobusuke Kishi, a prime minister himself from 1957-1960, served in the war cabinet of imperial Japan and was a paramount founding member of the LDP. 

Compared with Germany and Italy, which at least criminalized  Nazism and Fascism, Japan did not do the same thing. Figures like Mr. Abe and Ms. Takaichi are likely to continue emerging as long as Japan does not genuinely break from the past. There is uncertainty if it is possible.

She was a skilled anthropologist! She was the first to cover Donna Karan's debut collection in 1984: casually-comfy yet sexy pieces that women could wear to work and beyond. They still look fresh! But I had never heard of The Skimp, which apparently was a minidress invented by Halston in 1974. (Bobbi wrote that a proper Skimp was between 32 and 34 inches long.) Halston's sold for $260 (more than $1,700 in today's dollars) but, as Bobbi noted, department stores sold their own versions for $11. But do any of you who are "of age" remember a Skimp? I love her hair! Looking at Ms. Galli's hair is a reminder of how important it is for people with naturally curly/wavy hair to have a stylist who specializes in these hair types. 

I have a mixture of naturally curly/wavy hair. It wasn't always like that; I began getting curls around puberty, oddly. I blow dried it straight for years. Then about 20 years ago I decided to work with what I have. The largest struggle has been to find someone who knows how to cut and style natural curls and not leave me with the dreaded triangle-shaped hair. I've lived in several places in the last 24 years and I went through a few stylists before finding someone. Recently I found someone after only a year who specializes only in curls. She's a two hour drive from me, but she cuts it so well, it keeps its shape about four months (I've gone six), so worth the commute. I recently had my hair cut while on a road trip (I didn't have time to cut it before I left) and I found someone along the route with experience with curls and she also did a fantastic job. So I urge anyone having trouble getting the right cut to look for someone who specializes in curls/waves, or just try one to see the difference. I didn't know they existed. It has totally transformed my hair and my confidence, and I haven't had a bad hair day in a long time. My husband says the new cuts elevate my personality, give me a more exuberant look. He's very honest with feedback, too much so sometimes! so I'm careful with what I ask him!

I suspect that when the smoke has cleared that we may find that staff in Northern Ontario had to clear all external notifications, such as forest fire evacuation notices through their Head office in Toronto. This then resulted in hand wringing and delay or even failure to act. We increasingly see this desire at the top to control the message and to now blame the Federal Government for a local issue.

What we have seen in the past 20 years is an increasing lack of understanding of the geography and indigenous issues in Northern Ontario, although knowledge was never great. It is 1.5 hours by jet airplane from Toronto to Thunder Bay and then up to a 10 + hour drive to get to the end of the road depending where you are going. The view in the south is that 'the north' is a few hours drive from Toronto. There is little understanding of the size of the Province - about the size of Texas + Oklahoma and most of Kansas with few roads. Or France + Germany + Belgium and Holland.

When I mentored engineering staff for the Transportation Dept I would ensure that they got some understanding of  the northern issues by exposure through site visits and sometimes secondments. Unfortunately I doubt that is happening so easily today with an increasingly stingy attitude toward staff development and lack of appreciation of the geography.

To put some context on why these events are happening, just look at measured CO2 concentration in Earth's atmosphere from over a hundred years to recently:

year: CO2 concentration (mean)

1900: 294 ppm

1919: 302 ppm

1940: 308 ppm

1960: 317 ppm

1980: 339 ppm

2000: 370 ppm

2020: 414 ppm

2024: 425 ppm

Because humans burn over a 100 million barrels of oil every single day (plus all the coal, and natural gas), 
the CO2 from the burning all those fossil fuels accumulates 
(it takes a very long time to come out of the atmosphere, unlike methane).

And as CO2 concentration increases, Earth's average temperature increases (as does the ocean temperature).

And more importantly: for every one degree Celsius that Earth’s atmospheric temperature rises, the amount of water vapor the atmosphere can hold increases by about 7% 
(from Clausius–Clapeyron relation in thermodynamics). 

That means that a given parcel of air can suck up more moisture 
(and if not released right away) 
causes droughts; 

or,
 
if atmospheric forcing causes a sudden release: 
major flooding 
(like in the July 2025 Texas floods that killed a bunch of children). 

And as ocean temperatures rise, evaporation increases, and any "atmospheric river" flooding events that form become more intense.

Even worse is that hurricanes can become stronger and rapidly intensify.

This extreme weather will only get worse and worse.

We need to stop burning fossil fuels: adapting will get harder and more expensive.

Lettuce gets touched by many hands and things; with the current lack of govt inclination to help its citizens, I would not eat raw low growing plants. and no salads eating out.

The idea of those "black ships" being rowed by men in full armour, whatever the weather, is one of the movie's most ridiculous distortions. But then again, nobody expects Hollywood to show people going naked, even though that would have been both more plausible and more faithful to the iconography.

In the end, the film is a technical marvel. Everything else—story, acting, and characterization—is mostly hype. The real issue is that, if the movie followed the original narrative, audiences would quickly realize that Odysseus was a deeply unpleasant man (ask the slave women he order to execute after dealing with more than 100 suitors). And that's not a modern moral judgment. The Romans already saw him that way. Ask Virgil.

comments.name: Reuben
comments.body:
To explain why NewJeans mattered, success alone is not enough. K-pop was increasingly built around maximalism: huge drops, overstuffed concepts and songs designed to announce themselves instantly. NewJeans made restraint feel revolutionary. Their best records—“Attention,” “Hype Boy,” “Ditto,” “OMG” and “Super Shy”—were light, melodic and rhythmically subtle, drawing on 1990s and early-2000s R&B, UK garage and club music without sounding like museum pieces. Their voices worked as a group texture rather than a competition for the biggest note, while their videos made youth, friendship and ordinary life more vivid than another elaborate fictional universe.

My own K-pop hierarchy has BigBang and Blackpink as the two greatest groups, with Teddy Park’s production important to both. NewJeans would have deserved third place had their career not been interrupted and had they maintained that standard while developing. They had barely begun. The tragedy is not merely the music we missed, but the artistic growth that was arrested.

A great group changes without losing its identity. NewJeans appeared capable of that. A return without Danielle, and perhaps without the creative team that shaped them, cannot simply recreate 2022. But it is not too late. I hope everyone involved understands that NewJeans was not a formula or a name: it was a rare alignment of members, songs, production and visual imagination. Preserve that, and they may again release the best music in K-pop.

'IVORY: I drive S.U.V.s myself. I have kids; we need space.'

With due respect, this doesn't add up. Families used to be larger than today. 

In the fifties, a large family could squeeze into a station wagon. Not just in the USA, in Oz, NZ, the UK,

A-pillars back then were generally much narrower than today. 

A-pillars have widened in order to impart more structural strength and stiffness to the cabin, partly to improve safety in case of a rollover, by preventing the roof from collapsing.

Most cars in 50s were less powerful than today. They were also much more fun to drive. Automatics hadn't yet replaced stick shifts. Driving fast was a greater test of skill.

Today, cars are just auolmated giant boxes on wheels with aircon and entertainment systems stuffed in.

Very few drivers today, outside racing drivers, cab drivers, haulage drivers, construction drivers, et al, are as skilled as many amateur drivers were in the 50s.
